title: Characterising the set of deterministic quantum correlations in prepare-and-measure scenarios
authors: Nicola D'Alessandro, Oliver Karlsson, Carles Roch i Carceller
abstract: Correlations that do not admit a deterministic explanation are a central feature of quantum theory and a key resource for quantum information processing. Identifying and certifying such correlations, however, remains a fundamental challenge. In this work, we advance on this problem by considering deterministic correlations in the prepare-and-measure scenario consistent with a wide range of communication restrictions. To certify correlations incompatible with such deterministic models, we ask whether they admit a scenario in which measurement outcomes can be perfectly predicted by an adversary equipped with classical side-information. We show the usefulness of this approach and propose semidefinite programming relaxations tailored to three representative communication restrictions: fixed ensemble, bounded overlaps and restricted observables.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive framework to test whether observed correlations in prepare-and-measure quantum experiments can be explained by deterministic classical models. It achieves this by formulating constraints derived from three distinct physical assumptions—fixed ensembles, bounded overlaps, and restricted observables—into solvable Semidefinite Programs (SDPs). Success in solving the SDP implies determinism; failure proves genuine non-classicality.
main_problem: The core problem is characterizing the set of deterministic quantum correlations achievable in prepare-and-measure scenarios and developing methods to certify when observed correlations violate these deterministic bounds.
main_result: The authors propose using Semidefinite Programming (SDP) relaxations tailored to specific communication restrictions (fixed ensemble, bounded overlaps, restricted observables) to test for determinism. Infeasibility of the resulting SDP proves non-classicality.
method: The methodology involves formulating the problem as determining if observed correlations admit a deterministic explanation by introducing an adversary with full knowledge of shared randomness $\lambda$. This leads to solving feasibility problems via specialized SDP relaxations (e.g., Block Moment Matrix, Gram matrix).
model_or_system: The system is the prepare-and-measure scenario involving two parties (Alice and Bob), where Alice prepares states $ho_{\lambda}^x$ based on shared randomness $\lambda$, and Bob performs measurements $\{M_{\lambda}^b|y\}_b$. The analysis adapts techniques from Quantum Random Number Generation.
key_observables: The optimal guessing probability $p^g(x,y)$, which must equal 1 for correlations to be considered classical/deterministic.
important_parameters: Communication restrictions include Fixed ensemble (SE), Bounded overlaps ($	ext{S} eta$), and Restricted observables ($	ext{SO}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on solving SDP relaxations, which provide outer approximations of the true quantum set. Specific assumptions are made regarding how preparation states or measurements are constrained.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate critical visibilities and bounds (e.g., $	ext{W}_5$ vs. overlap parameter) comparing quantum maximums against classical bounds derived under different communication restrictions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically addresses the characterization of deterministic correlations by applying SDP techniques to three distinct physical assumptions: fixed ensemble, bounded overlaps, and restricted observables, building a hierarchy of necessary conditions for determinism.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous mathematical tools (SDP hierarchies) to quantify non-classicality in fundamental quantum tasks, which is crucial for understanding the resource theory aspects of quantum information processing beyond simple entanglement measures.
